title: That does not make freedom formal in the will alone, since every free act also springs from deliberation
source_text: XLV. Neque tamen inde consequens est, ut libertas dicatur esse formaliter in sola voluntate. Etenim quemadmodum omnis actio libera ortum suum voluntati aliquomodo debet, sic quoque omnis actio libera nascitur ex aliqua mentis consultatione, & deliberatione. Et sicut intellectus nullam actionem libere elicit quam non potuerit impedire voluntas, ita quoque nullus actus voluntatis liber est, de quo non licuerit menti consultare, atque deliberare. Unde sequitur aequo jure, ad mentem atque voluntatem referendas esse actiones liberas, ac proinde, si inde colligitur libertatem formaliter esse in voluntate, inde quoque colligi posse, illam formaliter esse in intellectu.
pass_a_gloss: Nor yet is it consequent from this, that liberty be said to be formally in the will alone. For as every free action owes its rise in some way to the will, so also every free action is born from some consultation of the mind, & deliberation. And as the intellect elicits freely no action which the will could not have hindered, so also no act of the will is free, about which it was not permitted to the mind to consult, and deliberate. Whence it follows by equal right, that free actions are to be referred to the mind and to the will, and therefore, if from this it is gathered that liberty is formally in the will, from this also it can be gathered, that it is formally in the intellect.
pass_b_english: It does not follow, though, that freedom should be said to be formally in the will alone. Every free action owes its origin in some way to the will, but every free action also arises from some weighing and deliberation by the mind.

The intellect produces no action freely that the will could not have prevented, and in the same way no act of the will is free unless the mind was able to weigh and deliberate about it. With equal right, then, free actions must be traced to both mind and will. If one concludes from the first point that freedom is formally in the will, one can conclude from the second that it is formally in the intellect.

choices.why: Elicere is the scholastic verb for a faculty's producing its own act; 'produces' gives the sense in plain English.
